name: Felix Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential. I’d like to hear what you would say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Felix Mensah, twenty-seven, and I lead a carpentry crew on building sites. I live with my partner Kofi in a rented place, and we have no children. I’ve saved a few months of expenses by keeping my spending plain, so I’m not one missed shift from trouble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me what a normal day looks like for you. What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the drawing and the delivery before I split the crew into cutting and fitting. I enjoy getting a complicated run of cabinets to line up without wasting boards. What wears me down is the strain on my shoulders and the paperwork after everyone else has gone home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say I’ll use a tool if it helps me catch a wrong measurement before the boards are cut. A carpenter still has to check the wall, because plenty of buildings don’t match the drawing exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t see a small change taking much of my site work away. I already have a modest cushion, and there are some crews nearby, so I can handle a short gap better than I could a few years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading my crew and try the measurement check on a small job before asking everyone to use it. I’d continue putting money aside when the contractor pays on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a minor tool change because I can test it without betting the whole job on it. I’d still pay attention to the work calendar, since a cushion can run down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare the tool’s measurement against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d measure the opening myself and compare it with the latest drawing before we order the frame. I’d also ask the person who surveyed the site whether a wall had moved since then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you feel you could absorb a short gap in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ve kept a few months of expenses in the bank, and Kofi and I don’t have children depending on our pay. I’d still watch our spending if a contract ended, but I wouldn’t assume one slow week means disaster.

say: I’ll use a tool if it catches a **wrong measurement** before we cut.
I still check the wall because **buildings differ from drawings**.
think: I don’t expect small changes to take much of my **site work**.
I can handle a short gap better now because I have **some savings**.
do: Keep leading my **crew** and test the measurement check on a small job.
Continue setting aside money from each **payday**.
feel: I feel **calm** about a minor change and keep an eye on the calendar.
S0.quote: A carpenter still has to check the wall, because plenty of buildings don’t match the drawing exactly.
fieldNote: Felix has a **measured approach** to software and wants a trial before wider use.
His moderate cushion makes a short gap manageable, though he knows savings can **run down**.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on current site jobs
Test the measurement check against a small site job
Continue saving part of each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office should use better order lists if they save the crew from waiting for a missing hinge. I don’t want a screen to decide a cut without checking what the site looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do some planning and record keeping as crew lead, and those tasks could be reduced. The hands-on side changes more slowly in this picture, but there’s still some risk to my hours if fewer people are needed for the thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the site manager to show me the new ordering and schedule tools on a job where the old process is familiar. I’d keep doing the fitting work and ask about my hours before signing up for any new monthly costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy because a part of my lead role may change, but the hands-on work still matters for now. My savings and a few nearby employers give me some room to respond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check first in that new schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the delivery time with the supplier’s confirmation and make sure it leaves time for our site check. If the sequence ignores drying time or an inspection, the crew still pays for the mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could faster office planning mean fewer sites open? What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card doesn’t say that, so I can’t make that claim. I’d watch whether the contractor actually cuts hours; some nearby crews still advertise, which gives me another place to ask if I need it.

say: I’d use **better order lists** if they stop the crew waiting for hardware.
I still check the site before a screen decides a **cut**.
think: I do planning and records as crew lead, and those **tasks could shrink**.
I worry some about hours, but I have savings and **nearby crews** to ask.
do: Ask the **site manager** to show me ordering and scheduling tools on a familiar job.
Check my **hours** before taking on new monthly costs.
feel: I worry about **reduced hours**, while savings and nearby employers give me options.
S1.quote: If the sequence ignores drying time or an inspection, the crew still pays for the mistake.
fieldNote: Felix looks for **practical evidence** before changing a familiar site routine.
His savings and several local crews reduce, but do not remove, possible **hours risk**.

steps.text: Keep doing fitting work on current site jobs
Learn ordering and scheduling tools with the site manager
Wait to add monthly costs until the contractor confirms my hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew not to treat a headline as a notice from the contractor. We should ask what is booked and what changes for next month’s hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take the records and planning in my crew lead job by 2028. Robots reach hands-on carpentry around 2031, so I can’t count on the physical side lasting forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d continue my work and hold onto the savings I already have. In 2029 I’d ask my contractor about the coming jobs and call other local crews if my hours had dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short, but I’m not starting from zero because the savings cover a few months. I’m anxious about losing hours and still believe I can make practical calls while there is time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You could call another crew, but robots are expected in 2031. Would that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d see it as a way to find work while there are openings, not as protection from the longer change. I’d rather use the savings to cover a short gap than pretend another builder has escaped the same timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost hours in 2029, what would you and Kofi change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause larger purchases and use part of the savings for rent and food while we looked at the next month. We don’t have children or a mortgage, so I’d avoid making a drastic move before checking what the contractor has booked.

say: I’d ask what work is booked instead of treating a **headline as notice**.
I’d want to know what changes for next month’s **hours**.
think: AGI could take the planning and records in **my lead job** by 2028.
Robots reach carpentry around 2031, so my physical work is not **permanently safe**.
do: Continue working and hold onto my current **savings**.
Ask my contractor about booked **work** in 2029.
Call **local crews** if my hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but my savings give me time to make practical calls.
S2.quote: I’d see it as a way to find work while there are openings, not as protection from the longer change.
fieldNote: Felix expects disruption to both **thinking and physical tasks**, while resisting catastrophic assumptions.
His savings can bridge a gap, but he does not assume a new crew is **protected**.

steps.text: Continue current site work while the contractor has projects
Keep the existing savings available for a job gap
Call other local crews if current hours fall in 2029
Pause larger purchases if income drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives the contractor time to explain changes and let crews practice with new systems. I’d want the crew to get the same information, rather than hearing different versions from different managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could handle the planning side in 2031, then robots would reach the hands-on work around 2034. I can use the extra years to save and learn, but there is no guarantee that my exact job continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the contractor’s new system with someone who knows it and keep leading the crew while jobs remain. In 2032 I’d review my hours and use my savings only if work slowed, rather than spend it all on an untested course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the eventual change, but five years lets me prepare without making a rushed decision today. The savings give me a little breathing space if a contract ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years before robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get three more years of hands-on wages after the 2031 date, if the work is still there. It is enough time to build savings and try training in small amounts, not proof that the site work is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move into construction planning as a long-term fallback after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t call it long term, since the card says AGI can do planning. I’d learn the tools that help now, then keep asking local builders what openings they actually have.

say: I’d ask the contractor to explain changes and give **practice time**.
I’d want every crew to hear the same **information**.
think: I expect AGI could take the planning side of my lead job in **2031**.
I can prepare, but my exact job has **no guarantee**.
do: Learn the contractor’s **system** with an experienced user.
Keep leading the **crew** while contracts remain.
Hold **savings** for a slowdown rather than spend on an untested course.
feel: I feel **anxious but not rushed** into a decision today.
S3.quote: The savings give me a little breathing space if a contract ends.
fieldNote: Felix values the extra time for **small steps**, not a large course with an unknown payoff.
He refuses to describe planning as safe when **AGI targets thinking work**.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s system with an experienced user
Keep leading the crew while contracts remain
Hold savings for a slowdown rather than spend on an untested course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is enough to plan sensibly, but people should still check whether the plan fits the jobs around them. I’d keep my standards high and learn tools when the contractor has shown they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have ten years to build more savings and learn the systems in use. Still, AGI reaches planning in 2036, then robots reach carpentry in 2039; I can’t assume a desk role or site job will be safe after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the crew’s work steady and put money aside each month. In 2037 I’d review the jobs available and my own hours, then speak with nearby contractors if my work had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a useful runway, and I’m less anxious than in the fast scenario. I still take the risk seriously because both sides of the trade face change in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to decide with Kofi before the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d agree how much to save and whether we still want to buy a place. We don’t have a child or wedding date to plan around, so we can make those choices based on our work and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in an expensive course with a decade to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with short training that the contractor supports and see if it helps me on site. I wouldn’t borrow a large sum for an office qualification when thinking work itself is what changes.

say: I’d plan for a decade, but check whether the plan fits **local jobs**.
I’d keep standards high and learn tools after the contractor shows they **work**.
think: I have time to build savings and learn the systems in **use**.
I can’t assume desk or site work stays safe after **both dates**.
do: Keep leading the crew’s **carpentry work** and save monthly.
Review local jobs and my **hours** in 2037.
Speak with nearby **contractors** if my work falls.
feel: I feel **less anxious** with a decade to prepare, while taking the risk seriously.
S4.quote: I’d say a decade is enough to plan sensibly, but people should still check whether the plan fits the jobs around them.
fieldNote: Felix responds to a longer horizon with **measured preparation**, not certainty.
He and Kofi consider buying a home without assuming **children** or a fixed date.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while carpentry contracts remain
Take short contractor-supported training that helps on site
Speak with nearby contractors if current work falls after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years leaves little time to make a plan before the office work changes. A clear view of the contractor’s projects and hours would help me and Kofi decide how much to save and whether to delay buying a home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask whether workers can get paid training during working hours. Learning matters, but if every course takes unpaid evenings, people with rent to cover have less chance to take part.

headlineQuote: Learning matters, but if every course takes unpaid evenings, people with rent to cover have less chance to take part.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** crew lead known for careful carpentry and sound site planning.
He lives with Kofi, earns typical pay for his job, and has **a few months saved**.
He is open to tools once they are proven on a real job and wants **clear responsibility** for checks.
Some local employers and savings give him room, though the long-term risk to **both task types** remains.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Felix most because the short warning leaves little time before thinking work changes.
whatWouldHelp: A clear view of **projects and hours** would help Felix and Kofi plan savings and a possible home purchase.
